newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania apologises for jailing, "selling" Germans.
newsitem.headline: Romania apologises for jailing, "selling" Germans.

text.p: Romania apologised on Thursday for deporting tens of thousands of ethnic Germans to labour camps during communist rule or "selling" them by demanding cash from the Bonn government for emigration permits.

"We express our deep regret and apologise for what happened," read the text of a declaration made public by Foreign Minister Adrian Severin at a news conference with his German opposite number Klaus Kinkel.
"This is a gesture of moral reparation for Romanian citizens and German citizens -- former citizens of Romania -- whose destinies remain definitively marked by such lamentable actions."
The declaration marked the first public acknowledgement that Romania under dictator Nicolae Ceausescu granted ethnic Germans exit permits in exchange for cash from West German authorities.

"Nicolae Ceausescu's communist regime resorted to a dishonourable bargain, claiming substantial financial compensation for reunifying ethnic German families from Romania who wanted to settle in Germany," the declaration said.

Ethnic Germans began settling in Romania eight centuries ago and numbered as many as 800,000 before World War One, mostly in the central Transylvania region and Banat near the Yugoslav border. Their numbers have dwindled to about 70,000.

Repression began during World War Two. After Romania switched from the Axis to the Allied side in August 1944, some 70,000 ethnic Germans -- men and women aged 16 to 40 -- were deported to labour camps in Siberia and coal mines in Russia and Ukraine.
As many as 20,000 are said to have died of hunger, cold and disease. Some were not released until 1956.
Mass emigration of a community then numbering 300,000 began in the early 1970s. Some 70,000 had left by December 1989, when Ceausescu was toppled and executed.
Another 100,000 followed in the next six years and many hit by post-communist poverty still want to go.
Secret documents published last year show that with Ceausescu in power, Romania amassed cash, cars and property in exchange for allowing Germans to emigrate.
Community leaders say West Germany paid between 5,000 and 12,000 marks for each of the 11,000 Germans who left each year.
Kinkel said the declaration "touches a very important question which affected our countries and peoples".
"We as German officials, want the German minority to stay here, but we have told them that if they believe they can have a better life in Germany, the door remains open for them."
Severin said the new centrist government, which ousted ex-communists in elections last year, wanted to denounce publicly the excesses of the Communist era.
"Such communist procedures are totally rejected by the new regime installed after December 1989," he said. "The present government strongly disapproves of these disturbing practices."
